runs.text: Soido, ou eſtrondo das aſas do paſſaro.

lines.note: Haoto is the sound of wings, explicitly described as a bird's wing-noise. The uo sequence belongs to the older spelling, not to the following hase verbs.

runs.text: Faxe, ſuru, eta, i. Faxiri, u.

lines.note: Hase is glossed by hashiri, running. The inflectional endings and explanatory i. are separate from the Portuguese sentence, whose ajun- continues below.

runs.text: taſe eſta raiz a muitos verbos como ſe vera a-

lines.note: The dictionary explains that this root attaches to many verbs. Both ajunta-se and abaixo cross physical row boundaries; neither fragment is a new entry.

runs.text: baixo, & da algũa força ao verbo ſignificando

lines.note: The prefixed root adds force to the verb. Significando leads into presteza, specifying speed rather than a separate lexical meaning on this row.
Presteza completes the explanation of haste. Item adds a causative sense, making something run, illustrated with a horse on the next line.
Uma wo hasuru means making a horse run. The printed fasuru is retained rather than expanded to an expected hasesuru; the Portuguese confirms the causative interpretation.
Haseai describes people meeting in haste. The contracted inflection is supported by the NINJAL headword, but its accent is not silently supplied where the local print is worn.
Completes com pressa, the manner of meeting in the preceding entry. It is not a modifier of the following haseatsumari headword.
Haseatsumari is gathering quickly. Atçumari represents intransitive atsumari, with -ru and -tta inflections, not the transitive atsume stem.

Haseage here concerns running a vessel aground, not simply raising something. Fune is a Japanese boat-word embedded in Portuguese; its slant here differs from the clearly Roman occurrence two rows below, so this occurrence remains italic.

runs.text: pedra, ou em algum baixo, &c. Vt,

lines.note: A rock or shoal is the obstacle the boat strikes. The final Fune begins the Japanese example and must join uo on the following row.
Fune wo se ni haseageta describes grounding a boat on a shoal. The second Fune is again embedded in Portuguese and printed Roman, unlike its italic surroundings.
Restinga completes the shoal or sandbank description. Its short standalone row is part of the boat example, not page furniture.
Hasearuki is running to and fro, literally combining haste with walking about. The final grave accent is visible in là, matching the de cà / pera là opposition.
Haseawase is causing a meeting or encounter. Its transitive force contrasts with haseai above and is expressed by Portuguese fazer encontrar.
Are ni haseawase, kore ni sashiawase gives successive encounters in combat. Sashiawase is a plausible distinct verb, not automatically changed to another hase compound.
Tatakōta completes the fighting example. Feiq. is the Roman Heike citation label; the following italic Portuguese identifies book four and begins the translation.

runs.text: contrandoſe ora com aquelle, ora com eſte.

lines.note: Completes encontrando-se: he fought, encountering now that opponent and now this one. This translation supports the alternating are/kore construction above.
Hasekaeri means returning quickly. The cayeri spelling represents kaeri and does not require a modernized kana-based spelling in Level 1.
Hasetsudoi describes many people assembling or coming successively. Its position before hasechigai is printed here and is not reordered to improve alphabetization.
Completes continuando, describing the continuing arrival of a crowd. The fragment belongs to hasetsudoi despite the intervening physical break.
Hasechigai means missing or passing one another while running. The scan contracts the nasal in desencontrar-se as õ, rather than printing a separate n after o.
Hasechiri is scattering in haste. Chiri is the intransitive scattering verb; the Portuguese subject is a multitude of people.
Completes the manner of scattering, com pressa. Its placement is distinct from the next entry's downward movement.
Hasekudari means descending quickly. Decer is the printed historical Portuguese spelling corresponding to descer, not an error to modernize.
Hasekuwawari means running to join others. The repeated u letters encode kuwawari; the Portuguese ẽ- begins entre and retains its contraction.
Completes entre outros, entering among other people. This establishes the joining sense of kuwawaru rather than merely passing them.
Hasefusagari is blocking a place by running into position. Fusagari supplies the obstruction meaning reflected by tapar and impedir.
Completes algum lugar correndo: some place is blocked while running. The split al-gum is Portuguese and not part of the next Japanese headword.
Hasei is wave-sound, clarified by nami no koe. This is a Sino-Japanese noun, plausibly 波声, not another compound of hase 'run'.
Haseiri is entering quickly. The explicit iru ending agrees with the entering verb and distinguishes it from neighboring forms with ordinary -ru endings.
Hasemairi is going or coming in haste. Mairi has the directional/humble verb sense; the worn middle letters agree with the NINJAL headword.
Hasemawari is going around quickly. Mauari represents mawari, and the Portuguese reinforces circular movement rather than arrival.
Hasemeguri likewise describes going around. The compressed utta ending is retained as printed and also appears in the NINJAL headword, rather than being expanded to megutta.
Completes going from here to there while running. The paired directional adverbs explain the range of the circling movement.
Hasemukai is running to meet or face someone. The meeting definition is consistent with mukau and the contracted open-o inflections.
Hasen means a damaged vessel, clarified as yabureta fune. This noun, plausibly 破船, is unrelated to the adjacent running compounds despite its similar beginning.
Adds 'or broken up' to the vessel definition. The physical fragment remains separate from hasenarabi below; no modern spelling is substituted.
Hasenarabi means proceeding abreast in haste. The contracted -ōda form is historically possible and supported by NINJAL, so it is not normalized to naranda.
Boats are given as the example of moving abreast. Funes is a Portuguese plural built on Japanese fune and is italic in this occurrence.
Hasenobori is ascending quickly. The ending otta combines with the preceding stem convention to represent nobotta, not a separate word.
Hasenobi means running ahead. The two listed past endings reflect alternative conjugational treatment, also preserved in the NINJAL headword; they are not collapsed to one modern form.
Completes passar diante, passing ahead. Although only one word long, this is the end of the hasenobi definition and is correctly associated with its own physical row.
Hasenuke is overtaking another person. Nuke gives the passing-through or getting-ahead sense specified by diante de outro.
Completes the overtaking definition by specifying running. The row belongs to hasenuke, not the arrival entry below.
Hasesanji means coming in haste, a compound with sanjiru/sanzuru. The final printed division mark separates com from pressa on the next row.
Completes com pressa at the foot of the column. It is body text rather than a catchword; the next column begins a new hase compound.
Hasesugi means passing ahead quickly. Sugiru supplies the passing-beyond sense, consistent with Portuguese avante.
Hasesusumi is advancing or pressing forward. Its -sumi/-sunda inflection is coherent and distinct from the preceding -sugiru verb.
Hasetaoshi means driving something down while running. The oita ending is retained as printed, not normalized to a modern taoshita form.
Takagishi yori uma wo hasetaoshite describes driving a horse down from a high bank. The Japanese object and source phrase agree with the following Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Derrubou, ou deitou em baxo o caualo corren-

lines.note: The translation describes bringing the horse down while running. Baxo is the historical printed form, and corren- continues into correndo below.

runs.text: do de cima de hũa rocha, ou lugar ingreme.

lines.note: Completes the descent from a rock or steep place. This confirms takagishi as the elevated bank or cliff rather than a personal name.
Hasetsuki is arriving at a run. Tsuku supplies arrival, with the listed past ending representing tsuita.
Hasetōri is running past or through. The touori spelling preserves the older vowel sequence rather than replacing it with an accented vowel.
Haseokure is falling behind while running. The printed wo spelling and nasal contraction in corrẽdo are retained independently of modern orthography.
Haseyose is bringing something close quickly. Chegar is used transitively here; the following row specifies the manner.
Completes the hastened bringing-near definition. The demonstrative manner-word aſſi belongs to Portuguese, not Japanese ashi.

runs.text: Dous paoſinhos com que comẽ os Iapoẽs.

lines.note: Hashi here means chopsticks, described as two little sticks used for eating. The following identical headwords represent different senses, not duplicate OCR lines.
This hashi is a bird's beak. Portuguese bico distinguishes it from chopsticks above and an edge below.

runs.text: Borda, ou cabo de algũa couſa.

lines.note: Hashi is an edge or end. Cabo, with a worn b visible in the scan, fits the definition; calo 'callus' would not explain this paired gloss.
Hashi is here a ladder or stair, an older lexical sense. It is not silently expanded to modern hashigo.
Hashi now means a bridge. Hashi wo watasu is constructing or laying a bridge across, not the intransitive crossing example below.

runs.text: ou atraueſar a ponte no rio. ¶

lines.note: The translation completes spanning the river. The next Japanese example begins hashi wo hi-, which continues as hiku on the following row.
Hi-qu gives hiku, removing the bridge. The next example hashi wo wataru switches to crossing it, preserving the transitive/intransitive contrast.
Crossing the bridge translates wataru. Hashi wo kakuru then introduces setting up a bridge, using the historical kakuru form rather than modern kakeru.
Completes armar, ou por ponte, erecting or placing a bridge. This short continuation is not an independent Japanese item.
Hashi/suru here concerns undoing completed accounts, not a bridge. The reference to hasan points back to the accounting entry; the terminal sign is retained without assuming modern spelling.
Hashibami is a kind of fruit or nut, plausibly hazel. The dictionary itself gives only this broad identification, distinct from the woodworking homonym below.
The woodworking hashibami consists of small boards inserted into others. En- begins encaixão, the fitting or jointing action continued below.

runs.text: caxão em outras nas bordas como em meſas,

lines.note: The boards fit into the edges of other boards, as in tables. This describes an edge joint or batten, not the nut of the previous entry.
The purpose is to prevent warping. Empenar has its woodworking sense here; the negative is essential to the explanation.
Hashibashi is the reduplicated edges or ends of something. The voiced second member bashi is reflected by b rather than a repeated faxi spelling.
Zaisho no hashibashi denotes the outskirts of a settlement. Arrabaldes supports the peripheral-place sense rather than literal objects' ends.
Lugar completes the settlement gloss. Item adds a small-amount sense; hashibashi wo begins the hearing example below.

The intended Japanese is kiita or uketamawatta, having heard only portions. The scan's damaged t was misread as i; qijta retains the visibly descending second vowel letter rather than silently normalizing it to qiita.
Completes hearing lightly or only a little of what happened. This translation makes the hearing-verb interpretation above much stronger than a literal reading of the original OCR qijia.
Hashibune is a small boat. The Portuguese compares it with a manchua and a little ship's boat, continuing across the row break.
Completes manchua, followed by batelinho. Both are vessel comparisons and do not belong to the measles entry below.
Hashika means measles; hashika wo suru is having the illness. The scan reads Sarampão with a, matching the repeated disease name on the next row.
Translates the Japanese illness expression as having measles. Its lowercase initial is independent of the capitalized noun on the preceding row.
A separate hashika, also nogi, is an awn of wheat or rice. The Portuguese botanical gloss prevents confusing it with the preceding disease homonym.
Hashikai describes something rough or harsh. The first illustration is coarse clothing against bare skin, with vestido split across rows.

runs.text: tido groſſeiro ſobre a carne nua, &c. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Completes vestido grosseiro, coarse clothing on bare flesh. The scan preserves a faint initial g and the long-s pair, not OCR rolleiro; Itẽ begins the additional brittle-material sense.

runs.text: Couſa facil de quebrar como ferro fraco, &

lines.note: Adds something easily broken, such as weak iron. This extends hashikai from surface harshness to brittleness rather than introducing a new headword.
Quebradiço completes brittle iron. Per met. marks a metaphorical human application: hashikai hito, a sharp or harsh person.

runs.text: Homem que da facilmente no coração de outro

lines.note: The person easily strikes another's heart or feelings. The following explanation specifies blunt speech, not a literal physical blow.

runs.text: falando logo o que ſente ſem reſguardo, nem

lines.note: Such a person immediately says what they think without restraint. Nem connects to brandura below, completing the absence of gentleness.
Brandura completes the harsh-speaking sense. Item then adds an acute, quick person, a potentially more positive intellectual sense of the adjective.
Completes veloz: quick in understanding and speaking readily. This belongs to the perceptive-person sense rather than the earlier brittle-material definition.
Hashikai ki is wood that breaks easily. Ki is the Japanese noun for wood; Portuguese pao is not normalized to modern pão.

runs.text: Lugar no theatro que eſta de bai-

lines.note: Hashigakari is the theatre passage or approach. The definition begins with its position below an arch; the physical bai- break belongs to debaixo.

runs.text: xo de hum arco por onde ſaem as figuras a pu-

lines.note: Performers emerge to public view through this arch or passage. Figuras refers to stage characters, not printed illustrations.
Completes publico in the theatre definition. The short row is body text and remains separate from the signature and catchword beneath it.
